B1:
Laura asked for her 10 payments to be met with "a high degree of certainty", which we took to mean a near-ironclad guarantee: on the day each falls due, no payment should depend on a share price, an interest rate or anybody else's money.

Laura is a graphic novelist, and her world has a habit that makes this easier to see. Comic pages are drawn twice – first in pencil, which can be rubbed out, then in ink, which is what gets printed. So in this report, ink is a dollar figure Laura already owns in Treasuries that will pay it on its date, and pencil is any figure no Treasury she owns will pay yet: her next advance, the 2028 deposit before it arrives, whatever her shares are worth, every forecast. A recession is one eraser across three pencil lines at once (her advances, share prices and co-sponsors' budgets), which is why a promised payment can't be left in pencil.

Most of each payment is inked in January 2027, when the first deposit buys 10 Treasuries, each maturing before the 1 January it pays. At the 6 November close that cost about $301,500, roughly the whole deposit.

The subtler problem was the time in between. The bonds pay interest along the way, and the February 2037 bond matures ten and a half months before its payment, so cash sits and waits, and a "certain" plan could quietly lean on future interest rates. That was the one pencil line left. The first $38,282 of the 2028 deposit inks it: $2,388 is the top-up that finishes the 10, and $35,894 buys extra Treasuries, so the payments are met even if waiting cash earns nothing at all. Publishers do the same with royalties, holding some back against returns until the risk passes – and if rates hold, most of this comes back to Laura too, about $45,500 in 2033 money.

By 1 January 2033 the operating reserve is about $444,500, roughly 111% of what the payments need. Our first plan, about three-quarters shares, missed a payment in 3.2% of model runs, and in 40.8% without the 2028 deposit. Buying the payments first never missed one.
B2:
Half of what Laura's shares are worth will never be promised to anyone. That half is her flexibility, and the IPS gave it three jobs: building costs that overrun, a stronger Taiwan dollar, or a co-sponsor falling short. On our central numbers it's about $21,300 in January 2033, and about $9,900 in a bad 1-in-20 future.

Is that enough? The Taiwan dollar is the one job we can test properly. A Taiwan dollar 10% stronger than in 2031 would need about $11,500 more, and her flexibility covers that in about 93 of 100 model futures – and in about 98 of 100 two-year stretches of the real Taiwan dollar since 1983.

So why half? Honestly, because we chose it. Keep only 30% back and Laura could promise about $10,000 more, but her flexibility would cover that stronger Taiwan dollar in only about half the futures. Keep 70% back and she promises about $10,000 less, with a bigger cushion and a narrower range. Each $5,000 more of promised top costs her about $5,300 of what she keeps, while the total she ends up with barely moves (within about $1,100 either way at the median). In other words, the split doesn't decide how much money there is – only how much of it is promised, and how much stays hers. Half is the middle of that trade, and no model picked it.

And there's a reason from Laura's own drawing desk. You can always add ink to a page, but you can't take it off cleanly – a mistake gets painted over, and the original keeps the record. A figure told to co-sponsors is the same: she can always give more than she said, never quietly less. So half the shares stay pencil on purpose, out of co-sponsors' sight, and anything the funds pay above her stated top goes back to her flexibility.

The catch is, building costs more often rise in the years shares fall, so her flexibility can be at its smallest exactly when costs press hardest. It's the one honest weakness in the design, and a good argument against trimming the cushion to make the promise look bigger.
B3:
In 2031 Laura has to give her co-sponsors two things: a dollar range for her facility contribution, and how confident she is in it. On today's figures that range is $95,000 to $115,000. The figures will move before then; the rule that produces them won't.

The bottom is fixed in January 2028, when the 2028 deposit buys the Treasury fund maturing in late 2032. That fund pays about $103,000 in 2033, and the bottom of her range sits below it. The top is fixed later, when the other half of the shares moves into Treasuries before the meetings. Both ends are rounded down, and 0.5% is held back as well. Printers work in much the same way: they run the art past the line where the page is cut, because the blade wanders, and keep the words well inside it. Laura's stated top is the cut line, the 0.5% and the rounding are the bleed, and the bottom sits safely inside.

Why say nothing before the shares move? Because until then the top is still pencil – it's just whatever the shares happen to be worth that week – and Laura only states a figure once it's inked. A number announced in 2029 could be out of reach by 2031, and the case is blunt that overpromising would damage her credibility. After the move, every dollar of her range is money she already owns, so the confidence part is easy: she can tell co-sponsors, quite truthfully, that she's certain.

We tested the range from both directions. Erase every pencil line – say the shares went to zero – and the page still reads: the 10 payments don't change, the floor still pays about $103,178, and the range becomes one figure, $95,000. Swap our forecast for someone else's and the top holds: of the fifteen investment houses that publish long-run forecasts for world shares, fourteen give the same $115,000 top under the rule. J.P. Morgan's 7.5%, the figure we used, sits in the upper third of them, not at the top.
B4:
On 5 October Darren argued that the world fund was a copout, and that we should be picking stocks and ETFs ourselves. A Taiwan fund, EWT, came up that day, and so did gold. We kept the one world fund, VT. Still, "copout" is a fair charge – a fund that owns everything looks like the one choice that needs no thought at all.

The first thing that stands out is how little that choice matters to Laura. In the plan's numbers, which shares she holds is worth about $800 to $1,600 to the outcome, while how the market as a whole does is worth $9,881 to $41,258 (1 in 20 each way). Picking would have meant working hardest on the smallest number in the plan.

EWT shows what picking costs in practice. It's about a fifth one company (TSMC, at 21.89%) and about three-quarters technology, and it charges 0.59% a year against VT's 0.06% – while VT already holds Taiwan, at about 3.5% of the fund. Gold answers inflation, which is a real problem, just not Laura's: her 10 payments are fixed in dollars.

The reason we like best is about checking our work. Comic artists used to draw their construction lines in a light blue the printing camera couldn't see, and our models, the 7.5% and every median in this report are like that: the judges see them, Laura's co-sponsors never will. With a whole-world fund, those blue lines aren't only ours. Fifteen investment houses publish long-run forecasts for world shares, and fourteen of the fifteen give the same $115,000 top on our rule. Our own picks would have had nobody else's lines to check against.

And a holding that needs no opinions keeps the IPS's promise that only two things can change the plan. When Barber and Odean (2000) studied 66,465 US households, the ones that traded most earned 11.4% a year, against the market's 17.9%. Picks need opinions, and opinions need revisiting.

So VT stayed. Darren was right that it's the easiest fund to buy; his argument is how we found out it's also the hardest one to argue against.
E1:
Laura asked for her ten payments to be met with a 'high degree of certainty'. The comfortable reading is a high probability in a model. Our first plan, about three-quarters shares, would have passed that test – it missed at least one payment in only 3.2% of our model runs. But that climbed to 13.7% if her 2028 deposit came in at $75,000, and 40.8% if it never arrived. That deposit comes from advances, speaking fees and licences – the same good years that lift shares. A plan that is certain only while her career goes well isn't what she asked for.

So we read it the strict way: no payment should depend on a share price, a forecast or anyone else's money when it falls due. Buying the ten payments first never missed one. At the close on 6 November that cost about $301,500, roughly her whole first deposit, and if yields fell a full point before January it would be nearer $334,000. Which sounds bad, but isn't: the 2028 deposit simply covers the difference.

The harder part was the small print. The bonds pay interest along the way, and the February 2037 bond matures ten and a half months before the 1 January 2038 payment it funds. Cash waiting like that earns whatever rates happen to be then, which quietly turns a locked plan into a bet on future interest rates. That's the job of the first $38,282 of the 2028 deposit: $2,388 is the top-up the IPS promised, finishing the ten, and $35,894 buys extra Treasuries, enough that the payments are met even if waiting cash earns nothing at all. If rates hold, most of it comes back to her.

The iBonds funds (IBTM to IBTR) pay out what their bonds are worth, not a fixed sum – close, not exact – and the margin covers that too. By 1 January 2033 the operating reserve should be about $444,500, about 111% of what the ten payments need, all of it bought by January 2028: five years before the first payment goes out, and fourteen before the last.
E2:
The obvious move with the shares would have been to promise all of them. Co-sponsors like a big number, and Laura wants to give as much as she responsibly can – so why hold half back? Because 'responsibly' is carrying a lot of weight in that sentence. The IPS names three things that can go wrong once the building is under way: costs that overrun, a stronger Taiwan dollar, a co-sponsor who falls short. Half the shares, promised to no one, is the money for those – about $21,300 in January 2033 on our central figures.

Is that enough? For the currency, mostly. If the Taiwan dollar is 10% stronger than in 2031, the building needs about $11,500 more. Her flexibility covers that in about 93 of 100 futures we modelled, and in about 98 of 100 two-year stretches of the real Taiwan dollar since 1983 – which we trust a little more, since it actually happened.

Now the cost, because there is one. Every $5,000 more she promises at the top costs her about $5,300 of what she keeps. Keep only 30% back and she could promise about $10,000 more, but the cushion would then cover that currency move in only about half the futures. Keep 70% back and she promises about $10,000 less, with a fatter cushion and a narrower range. Yet the total barely moves – at the median, within about $1,100 either way. The split doesn't change how much money there is, only how much of it is promised. Half is the middle of that trade, and we chose it; no model did, and we won't call it optimal.

One honest caveat: this cushion is not a hedge. Building costs more often rise in the years shares fall, and a recession is also when co-sponsors trim their budgets, so the cushion can be thinnest just when it's needed most – about $9,900 in a bad 1-in-20 future. That's why none of it is promised: co-sponsors never hear about it, so in a bad year it can shrink without costing Laura anyone's trust.
E3:
In 2031 Laura sits down with people about to commit their own money and tells them how much she'll put in, and how sure she is. If she overshoots, the damage isn't a few thousand dollars – it's the credibility the whole residency is built on, and co-sponsors remember. So her range isn't a forecast. It comes out of a rule, and on today's figures the rule gives $95,000 to $115,000, with $115,000 as the central contribution.

The bottom is the easy end. The Treasury fund bought in January 2028 matures in late 2032 and should pay about $103,000 in 2033, and $95,000 sits comfortably beneath that. From the day that fund is bought, the bottom is fixed. Push it to the extreme – every share she owns goes to zero – and the ten payments don't change, the floor still pays out, and her range simply becomes one figure: $95,000.

The top is where VT comes in, and it's why Laura says nothing until half the shares have moved into Treasuries. Until then, markets can push the top up or down as they please, and any figure she quoted would really be a guess about where the world's markets will sit a few months later. If they fell after the meeting, she'd be the one explaining the gap, to people who'd planned around her number. After the move, the top is money she owns, in Treasuries. She isn't predicting anything by then – she's reading her own statement.

So how sure can she be? Of the range she actually announces, completely. Both ends are in Treasuries, both are rounded down, and anything the funds pay above the top goes to her flexibility rather than to anyone she's made a promise to. What stays uncertain is only where the top lands, and that's a question about the next few years of world markets – one Laura never has to answer in public until the answer is already sitting in her account.

C1: We know Treasury bonds (including this one – maturing 2037) won't create wealth, but they will remove uncertainty, through duration-matching. In other words, we take Laura's requested 'high degree of certainty' to mean a near-ironclad guarantee, and we provide exactly that. Every year the bonds sit untouched is a good year – one less year of Laura's money being exposed to anything the restless markets might decide to do. Notably – Laura's payments are fixed in nominal dollars, so a nominal Treasury matches the liability perfectly, meaning we don't need TIPS, which would hedge against a nonexistent inflation risk.
C2: Some years, WInS lists no Treasuries maturing – so we purchased iShares iBonds (like IBTM for 2032) instead. Defined-maturity, investment-grade, liquid, cheap and transparent about yields, these behave a lot like bonds when held to their end – so we'll simply ignore price noise in the interim. Together, our T-Bonds and iBonds ensure each of Laura's payments rests on a dedicated instrument (not merely a forecast). The catch is, their terminal payout is a net asset value, as opposed to a promise of par – but in return we gain a level of liquidity which no odd-lot bond offers.
C3: VT is where we allow ourselves to be wrong – because it's the only investment not standing between Laura and a payment deadline. This ETF owns thousands of companies, diversified across countries and sectors, which means we can avoid paying the price for the vain illusion that we can pick winners, instead buying the entire market's growth premium at an expense ratio of just 0.06%, for a forecast return of about 7.5% a year (as per JPMorgan). The T-Bonds and iBonds already cover the operating commitments, so VT answers a different question – how generous can the facility contribution be?
X1: Pension funds cover fixed payments either by matching their bonds' average life to the payments and rebalancing as rates move, or by buying one bond per payment and holding it. We do the second, which needs no forecast or trading. In January 2027, her first $300,000 buys a ladder of Treasury bonds and Treasury funds with fixed end dates, each maturing just before a January payment. A Treasury held to maturity pays exactly what it promised, whatever markets do, so no payment depends on shares.
X2:
In 2031, Laura gives co-sponsors a range. The bottom is the floor, rounded down: money she already owns. The top adds half her shares, which move into Treasuries before she names it, because a number said aloud can't quietly be halved after a bad year. The other half stays hers and liquid, as a cushion if the building costs more in Taiwan dollars.

The ladder's one weakness is that it counts on reinvesting its bonds' interest; if rates fall and stay low, it can fall short. Before Laura names her range, we price that shortfall at the day's rates, add a margin, and move that much from her kept shares into Treasuries. Her spare money shrinks before her promise does, and if it can't cover the gap, the whole range comes down.
